title: The ordinary believer
hookLine: history is kings, but faith was carried by mothers, farmers and traders

cards: In Medina, in the Prophet's mosque, someone used to sweep the floor. The narrator of the hadith isn't even sure whether it was a man or a woman.
One day the Prophet, peace be upon him, noticed the sweeper was missing and asked. People told him the sweeper had died and been buried; they hadn't thought it worth telling him.
He asked them to show him the grave, and he went and prayed there. A sweeper whose name the record didn't keep, and a prophet who walked to the grave. Today: the ordinary believer.

teach.b: First, notice what that story in Sahih al-Bukhari keeps and what it drops. It keeps the work and the visit. It drops the name.
Second, look at who the chronicles name: caliphs, sultans, generals, the occasional well-known scholar. That's what chroniclers wrote down. But a faith doesn't survive on coronations.
Someone had to teach a child the opening surah at a kitchen table. Someone had to stop work at the edge of a field when the time for prayer came.
Someone had to carry the prayer across the sea in a trader's head, and keep it in a port town far from home. Mothers, farmers, traders, sweepers. Mostly unnamed.
Third, the tradition itself points the light at them.

teach.h: GOD LOOKS AT HEARTS AND DEEDS.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet saying that God does not look at your bodies or your appearance, but at your hearts and your deeds. Not your title. Not your wealth.

Fourth, take that lens back through the reigns this path has named. The bond Ibn Khaldun wrote about lives or dies in ordinary friendships. Even yesterday's scholars learned their first letters from someone.
Under every ruler this path named, unnamed people were raising children, working fields, teaching the prayer. The history books are thin on them. The faith isn't.

how: Muslims often learn their first surahs and the prayer from parents and grandparents at home, and some pray for the forgiveness of their teachers and parents by name.

o: the record of a sweeper's name in Medina
a book listing the caliphs and their reigns
a major collection of the Prophet's sayings

games.q: the ordinary believer — tap the pairs.
p: buried without the Prophet being told
asked to see the grave and prayed there
God looks at hearts and deeds

s: the narrator of the hadith was sure whether the sweeper was a man or a woman
the narrator wasn't sure. the record kept the deed, and the Prophet's visit, not the name.
the people told the Prophet about the sweeper's death right away
they buried the sweeper without telling him, thinking it too small a thing; he asked to see the grave.
a hadith says God looks at hearts and deeds, not appearance
Sahih Muslim reports that God does not look at bodies or appearance, but at hearts and deeds.

games.q: you're the Prophet. you learn that the person who swept your mosque died and was buried, and nobody told you. what do you do?
o: ask to be shown the grave, and pray there.
send a message of thanks to the family later.
games.why: the hadith in Bukhari says he asked them to show him the grave, and went and prayed there.

practice: Bring to mind one person who passed something good on to you and will never be in a history book: whoever taught you a prayer, or how to be kind, or how to keep going.
See their face, their hands, the room where it happened, and stay with them a while. If you pray, ask God's mercy for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Sahih Muslim, the hadith collection that keeps the Prophet's saying that God looks at hearts and deeds, not bodies or titles. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: ordinary hands carried it. The record kept the work, not the name. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 458 (the person who swept the mosque; the Prophet prays at the grave)
